On October 3, 2025, Governor Gavin Newsom signed SB 403, a bill that makes California’s End of Life Option Act permanent.

On January 9, 2024, Assemblymember Herb Conaway introduced bill A1880, which waives or reduces the waiting period between requests for medical aid in dying if the person is not expected to survive that time frame

On February 7, 2025, HB 1876 was introduced by Rep. Skyler Rude and Rep. Strom Peterson to improve Washington’s Death with Dignity Act; the bill had a hearing on February 14, 2025, but did not advance.
On June 5, Governor Jared Polis signed the improved End-of-Life Options Act into law. SB 68 goes into effect August 7, 2024.

On July 13 2023, Gov. Tina Kotek signed House Bill 2279, bipartisan legislation introduced by the Oregon Health Authority to repeal the residency restriction in the Oregon Death with Dignity Act. The bill took effect immediately, making Oregon the second state after Vermont to…

On March 15, 2023, the House floor heard the Third Reading of SB 471, and it unanimously passed (66-0), clarifying that healthcare providers are able to refuse to participate in Medical Aid in Dying for reasons of conscience. The law was signed by Governor Lujan Grisham (D).
Medical aid in dying is currently authorized in Hawai‘i. Legislation to improve the Our Care, Our Choice Act (OCOCA) passed and was signed by Governor Josh Green on June 2, 2023
On June 23, 2025, LD 613 was signed into law by Governor Janet Mills modernizing Maine Death With Dignity Act.

Montana’s Supreme Court ruling in 2009 made medical aid in dying legally permitted, but the legislature has never passed a law to codify it (HB 637 failed) and also rejected a bill that would have criminalized it, so the practice remains legal only because of the court decision
The law cannot be utilized until the regulations are completed by the State Department of Health and Social Services or January 1, 2026, whichever comes first.
On Tuesday, May 2, 2023, Vermont Governor Phil Scott signed H. 190, removing the residency requirement from the state’s medical aid-in-dying law.
